fields.title: Amdahl's Law Explained Simply
fields.keyTakeaway: The gain from speeding up a component is limited by its share of the total time, so an optimization task starts with calculating its share, not with an idea.
fields.sections/0/blocks/0/text: We sped up a component by half. Why did the screen get faster by only 6%?
fields.sections/1/blocks/0/text: Optimizing the wrong component is the easiest way to waste weeks. The rule to prevent this is stated in one line and almost never applied.
fields.sections/2/blocks/0/text: [[amdahls-law|Amdahl's law]] in product terms: **the speedup of a part is limited by that part's share of the whole.**
fields.sections/2/blocks/1/text: A component takes 12% of the time. We sped it up twofold—we gained 6% overall. Sped it up threefold—8%. Even instant execution yields 12%, and physically more is impossible.
fields.sections/2/blocks/2/text: Hence the prioritization rule: **first calculate the share, then decide if it is worth it.**
fields.sections/2/blocks/4/text: [[bottleneck|The bottleneck]] is the component with the largest share. Once it is removed, the next one becomes the bottleneck, and this is normal: optimization is a sequence, not a single action.
fields.sections/2/blocks/5/text: Second corollary, less obvious: **on the critical path, only the work that lies on it matters.** Speeding up a parallel call that is not the longest yields nothing at all.
fields.sections/3/blocks/0/text: An example of a failed optimization that became a lesson. The team spent two weeks speeding up response serialization: it was 90 ms, became 30. The actual screen improvement was 2% because serialization took 3% of the time.
fields.sections/3/blocks/1/text: That same week could have been spent reducing the response size, which took 17%.
fields.sections/3/blocks/2/text: After this, a rule was introduced: **before an optimization task, the description must state the component's share and the maximum possible gain.** Tasks without these numbers do not enter the sprint. Over six months, the rule filtered out five tasks and redirected three.
fields.sections/3/blocks/3/text: Reverse case: response transmission took 17%, client images took 34%. Working with images yielded a 22% improvement in four days.
fields.sections/4/blocks/0/text: The share changes after every improvement, and priorities must be recalculated. What was 8% can become 25% after removing the main bottleneck.
fields.sections/5/blocks/0/text: The gain from speeding up a component is limited by its share of the total time, so an optimization task starts with calculating its share, not with an idea.
